utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cvetic. Please sit down. The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth still applies, of course. And Mr. Stamp is continuing his questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cvetic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to start today by showing you a document and asking you to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's 00 -- sorry, 01991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a MUP staff meeting of 21 December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall attending that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I see here that one of the attendees apart from the minister and Lieutenant-Colonel-General Obrad Stevanovic is Ilic, Dragan Ilic. Do you recall seeing him from time to time in Kosovo during 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1998, yes; but during 1999, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remind us of his office, or the office he occupied?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dragan Ilic was head of the administration of crime police of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the seat office was in Belgrade, I take it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And can you say who his immediate superior would be in the chain of command, so to speak, in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said yesterday, the crime police administration belonged to the public security sector, which means that his immediate superior was head of the public security sector. Besides, in the ministry, there was also an assistant minister who was in charge of the crime as such, and he was also superior to General Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at page 2 of the document in English. And I think it's at the bottom of page 1 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see in the last paragraph part of a speech by the Minister Stojiljkovic, and it says in the last sentence here: "According to the agreement," that is the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement, "we should not allow them," them being the OSCE mission, "access to any military or police facility." Do you recall the minister issuing those instructions or conclusions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this meeting the minister said that we should cooperate with the OSCE mission, that we should provide all the information relating to terrorist activities to the OSCE mission, and that there was no reason for us not receiving members of the OSCE mission or talking to them as regards all the issues or problems at Kosovo. On that occasion, Minister Stojiljkovic said that this is a verifying mission, that the goal of this mission was to establish the real facts of the situation in Kosovo, that this was not an inspection mission, and that because of this, as police force, we are not obliged to justify ourselves to them. And indeed in that context he said that we do not need them to allow them to access any military facilities, any storage facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were those directions or directives complied with in the SUPs in Kosovo in time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say whether these instructions were entirely complied with by all the SUPs in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, but as pertains to the SUP Kosovska Mitrovica, none of the verifiers ever asked me to come into any of these storage facilities where we kept military equipment and weapons. We only discussed the issues pertaining to terrorism and their personal security.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move to another document. This is P8 -- sorry, I'd like to tender 0991 [sic] and ask that it be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1043, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now could we move on to P85. That's 65 ter number 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Seems to be a very important meeting, so perhaps with the assistance of the usher I could hand you a copy so you could peruse it. These are the minutes of a meeting of the Pristina MUP staff on the 17th of February, 1999. That is shortly before the NATO intervention and coming up to a very important period. And we see here from these minutes the list of attendees included the most --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This introduction and explanation by Mr. Stamp is rather lengthy. I believe he should proceed with asking a question, nothing was said about this document as yet and he is already qualifying it in a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Djurdjic, between us we can cope with Mr. Stamp. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see present in attendance, if you read the first few lines, the minister, the head of the RDB, and the head of the RJB, as well as assistant Minister Stevanovic is present. You see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And also I see --

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is quite all right. I was present at this meeting and I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. That would have been my --

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say that I know in person all -- everybody who was present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's start by looking at the opening presentation by General Lukic. If we see early in the presentation, and I think it's about 10 lines down in both the English and the B/C/S from the beginning of the presentation - he says that: "RPO," and again this is improperly translated in the document in English as reserve police station, "reserve police squads or units in nearly all villages inhabited by Serbs are very active. The service has increased its activities in towns." And later on in the same presentation at the bottom of page 1 in the English version, he says that: "On Saturday, the 20th of February, 1999, a meeting of the staff will be held with all police unit detachment commanders for further consultations about their engagement. Meetings have been held with all the RPO, and they were attended by General Momcilo Stojanovic and Lieutenant-Colonel Blagoje Pesic." I think yesterday you told us that you knew Lieutenant-Colonel Pesic. Did you know General Stojanovic, Momcilo Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, General Lukic is here speaking about a plan that had been worked out including three mopping up operations, and in the context of what he is saying about that plan, he says that there were consultations with these RPOs about their engagement. Can you comment on this? What were or what was the planned engagement or use of the RPO in respect of these mopping up operations that General Lukic was speaking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought that Mr. Stamp was going to stop with his compilation of everything. It's all written down here and the witness can comment on it. But what Mr. Stamp just stated is not -- are not the contents of this very document, so I'd rather have Mr. Stamp ask questions rather than quoting parts of the document and making a compilation which is not really what the document says. I believe that this is not appropriate for direct questioning, not even for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, there is something in what Mr. Djurdjic says.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could be kind enough to try to be accurate in your references to the minutes, but we are more interested in what the witness says than what counsel says about a document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, I quoted parts of the documents in order to focus you on what I'm interested in hearing you comment on, and that is the engagement of the RPOs. What was General Lukic speaking about? How were the RPOs expected to be engaged in these operations that he is referring to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The RPOs were formed exclusively to defend inhabited areas or settlements. They were formed upon military principles so they had a commander, a deputy commander, and a certain number of members. These reserve police squads or RPOs were not mobilised at all times, so this was not a peacetime formation, but they were only mobilised when needed. And their task was to prevent the entry of Siptar terrorist forces into settlements. Whenever there were operations that were planned at the level of the Joint Command with participation of the army and the police, then reserve police squads were also engaged. Over the previous two days we could see that orders for the implementation of anti-terrorist activities included RPOs when referring to armed non-Siptar population, so these were Serbs that were armed and were organised within reserve police squads. And they were engaged only on the as-needed base, and only in the territory in which they lived. They were never moved to other territories. They were not parts of manoeuvre structure of any units, but rather part of territorial structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very good. And General Lukic also said, just about at that point, and I'll quote it because this is the part I want you to focus on: "A plan of the RJB has been worked out to prevent and thwart the entry of NATO troops into our territory. The staff plans, when it is ordered, to carry out three mopping-up operations in the Podujevo, Dragobilija and Drenica areas and has allotted around 4.000 policemen, around 70 policemen of the operative," and this would be operative pursuit group, the OPG, "and around 900 police reservists. The staff plans when it is ordered to carry out this plan." Who or what body would give the order to activate or to carry out the plan?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February, that was the time when negotiations at Rambouillet initiated, and in that period there were certain problems, certain difficulties at the talks in Rambouillet. So the estimate was made by the top leaders of the state that there could be a possible threat of NATO aggression, and that because of this, we should start with adequate preparation in the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia including obviously Kosovo and Metohija. What were the goals of this estimate? The estimate said that NATO pact forces were being amassed in Macedonia and that a land invasion was to be expected from the direction of Macedonia. For that reason, it was necessary to increase the combat readiness and mobility of the military and police units to a higher degree. And for this reason, General Lukic said that we do have plans prepared and if any combat activities should begin, if an aggression should indeed take place, that actions of mopping up will begin, that is, anti-terrorist activities will begin in Drenica district; Malisevo district; and Sajske [phoen] district, so the place that is mentioned here, Podujevo, that belongs to the Sajske district. So indeed the forces were prepared and these numbers that he stated here are also correct. So this is all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, thanks for your answer. We have a lot to go through today so I'm going to ask you if you could be a little bit more brief and direct in your answers. The question I asked you is this: Who was General Lukic referring to when he said these mopping up operations in Kosovo would be carried out when it was ordered? Who would give the orders to proceed with the mopping up operations in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija which was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we go further and look at page 3 in the English. And I think that's in the middle of page 3 in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just want to focus on one part of the presentation of the Minister Stojiljkovic. And that's at the end of the first paragraph of this presentation, Mr. Cvetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's the last line in the first paragraph of page 3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which I'll just read: "Within two or three days of an attack we have to put our plans in motion and use the time to clear the territory of terrorists." Do you recall the minister saying that at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was the plan. After the first NATO bomb fell, this was to be a signal to launch a very decisive action of destroying all the Siptar terrorist forces in the territory of Kosova-Metohija, and this activity was to be completed within three days. And after the NATO aggression started, the activity was launched, but it wasn't completed within three days because this time estimate was unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it also launched in Drenica area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the whole territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at the bottom of page 3 on the copy you have? And this is the middle of page 3 in the English translation. We see the minister, among the forthcoming tasks that he refers to is that he says: "Approach and engage volunteers carefully, linking their engagement through the reserve police force when assessed as necessary." Firstly, was it, in your understanding as SUP commander within the -- was it lawful to engage volunteers into the police force in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say this: Not just the head of the SUP, but no one in the MUP and no one in the other structures of the system of defence can engage volunteers except the Army of Yugoslavia. The law is quite explicit there. In Article 15, namely, of the Law of the Army of Yugoslavia provides that the Army of Yugoslavia in the event of immediate or imminent danger or danger of war, can be replenished with volunteers. Can be. The law does not permit the option to engage volunteers it to any other structure in the system of defence other than the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he said the engagement should be linked to the reserve police force. What reserve police force is this we are referring to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot provide an adequate response here as to what the minister meant, what reserve police. The police reserve was part of the RPOs and the reserve police forces which supplemented the active police forces up to their full strength, according to establishment. I don't know exactly which police reserves he had in mind, but regardless of what he was thinking of, this was not something that was in accordance with the law. Let me be precise, to the law that was in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And before we move away from this document, we should probably for completion observe at the end of the document we see that General Djordjevic made a presentation and said that five officers were to be given a promotion, et cetera. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Promotions of reserve, or rather, police superiors were successive. Some were done according to regular procedure, and some according to extraordinary procedures. On this occasion, he said that it was necessary to promote to a higher rank five senior officers according to an extraordinary procedure. And there is also a decision that he handed down to those -- or there was a decision referring to the promotion of those five superiors, but I don't remember who they were. At that meeting, I was really just concentrating on those tasks and duties that the ministry was facing to prepare in the event of a possible aggression, what the minister was saying about what had to be done and how this had it to be translated into the work plans of the Secretariat. All that was said on the 17th of February, 1999. On the following day, the 18th of February, was sent to the Secretariats in a dispatch in 20 paragraphs what were the duties and who was going to be in charge of what. Not only the Secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija, but to all the Secretariats in the Republic of Serbia including the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, thank you. As you have gone there, perhaps we could move on from that document to the dispatch that you spoke of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at 04086, and it's P356. If we could move through it. Just browse it from page 1 to page -- the end, if we could. Could we just move to the end. Could the usher assist me to hand the witness a hard copy of this document and return the previous one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think if you go to the end of that document, Mr. Cvetic. If we could do the same in English. Who signed or issued that dispatch, and is that the dispatch you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is that dispatch of the 18th of February, number 312. And the dispatch was signed by the deputy minister and chief of the public security department, Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic, and this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see -- since we are there, you see at item 20 he orders you or reminds you of your duty to report up the movement of NATO and other forces and also other incidents of interest?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to page 2 on your copy, and I'm talking about paragraph 7. And this is at the top of page 3 in the English translation. He said: "Through intensified intelligence and other measures and actions, carry out the necessary checks, compile lists, and establish complete control over volunteer and paramilitary units and their members." You recall those instructions being a part of the dispatch that he sent out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but what is meant is that the state security service, which received this Dispatch 312, and all the Secretariats in the Republic of Serbia, are to be engaged in their operative work using their connections, collaborators, and others to keep an eye on all of those volunteers and members of the paramilitaries who had previously taken part in combat in the territory of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and to go through their precise records, and to place them under control so that their movements are known; or as we would say in police jargon, to just cover them operatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you told us earlier that this dispatch reflected what the minister had said at the meeting the day before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the meeting the day before, the minister had said -- if I could find it again. "Approach and engage volunteers, carefully linking their engagement through the reserve police force." Was a subsequent order issue by General Djordjevic in furtherance of the minister's instructions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't understand what is not quite right here. The volunteers cannot be used in units of the MUP, but only as part of the Army of Yugoslavia. What is stated in paragraph 7 that the coverage and taking of other actions should be applied to check the records and to keep an eye and complete control over volunteers and members of the paramilitaries, to keep them under control. This includes all 33 of the Secretariats in the territory of Serbia and the state security department. It was their duty for each one them to establish if there were any paramilitary formations members in their territories who had previously participated in combat in the fronts in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if there were any volunteers in their area, and to keep a record of all those volunteers, and to place them under control. I don't know if all the Secretariats did that or not, that is another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, but what I'm asking you is whether if the instructions given to you by General Djordjevic in paragraph 7 is in furtherance of the instructions or the statements made by the minister at the meeting day the before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister talked about general matters. Matters of concept and doctrine. These are then assignments from that estimate given by the minister. These are now the tasks or conclusions based on all of that. I really couldn't say until I really have a look at everything that the minister had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to look at what the minister said. Could we move on to 4077. And that is P702. This is a dispatch on 24th of March from the Minister Stojiljkovic. And if perhaps you could get a hard copy to the witness, with the assistance of the usher. I think this copy here on the monitor is not very clear, and we can also retrieve the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could look at the second page, item 9 of the minister's dispatch, just to remind ourselves. You'll see in item 9 that the minister again emphasised the importance of reporting up to the ministry headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it is best, since the copies we have in Serbian are not very good, if we could probably expand -- pan in on item 9 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You recall the dispatch and recall the minister again emphasizing the importance of reporting up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we move to page 1, the front, first page in the English -- no, no, I think it's the same page in the B/C/S. If we could keep the B/C/S there and try to expand paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the minister is reminding you that you: "Shall register all volunteer and paramilitary units and their members and keep them under control in case that you might need to engage them."

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is linked to the Dispatch 312 signed by the chief of the public security department based on the address of the minister on the -- at the meeting of the 17th of February where it says -- where he said that all Secretariats in the Republic of Serbia needed to establish the situation in their territory regarding all the paramilitary and volunteer units existing in their area. And now it says to make a record, establish control over them and their members in case it would be necessary later to engage them. So in a way it's a possibility in the future. Not that they would be engaged, but they could possibly be engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And you said it relates to the dispatch from the chief of the public service department. If you go back to the front page, the first paragraph of this dispatch, we will see that the minister explicitly refers to the dispatch of General Djordjevic where he says that you "were ordered as per our dispatch number 312 of the 18th of February." So the minister explicitly refers back to that previous dispatch. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is all accurate and it's all logical. And I can explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please go ahead. But briefly, if you may.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting on the 17th of February, the minister spoke about the overall security situation and measures that had to be taken in the case of imminent threat of war or war that are expected of all the Secretariats. Then on the 18th of February, a dispatch was issued, number 312, where all the tasks are specified on the basis of that speech. This dispatch signed by Minister Stojiljkovic especially emphasises this issue of operations to establish the situation regarding all the paramilitary and volunteer units in their respective areas. I.e., to pay special attention to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I just was asking if you noted that he, in reference to the dispatch signed by General Djordjevic, he says "our dispatch"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know, the witness did answer, and now if Mr. Stamp maybe doesn't like this answer, he cannot go back for the third time to ask the witness to reply to the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And for purposes of time, I think we should move on. Do you recall after that, the 24th of March, General Djordjevic attending meetings of the MUP staff or meetings of the police leadership in Kosovo while you were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 24th of March, yes, and only at one meeting held on the 16th of April, 1999, while I was in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall attending a meeting on the 8th of March, 1999, of the leadership of the police in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall who the attendees were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister was there, the chief of the sector of the public security, the state security, the PJP, and the chiefs of the SUP, and the Chief of the General Staff. The MUP staff in Pristina. This was on the 8th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That was the chief of the sector of the public security that was General Djordjevic; and state security is General Markovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could briefly tell us in a sentence or two at the most, what was the purpose of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the estimate of the degree to which the territory was endangered, or the military political assessment of the situation, indicated that there was a danger of aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that it was necessary to undertake measures and activities for eventual defence from the aggressor and to take measures possibly to annul the actions by the Siptar terrorist forces. But fear began to spread among part of the population in Kosovo and Metohija, and a large number of Serbs began to move out. Propaganda also played a part in this, and the minister particularly referred to this matter saying that the Serbs should not submit to this propaganda, that they should remain at their homes, and that the organs of the Ministry of Interior should not accept requests for registry of change of residence. They should not enable people to register changes of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you finish your answer or did I interrupt? But I hope you can be brief.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, other measures were also mentioned regarding preparedness, mobilisation, protection of the population, evacuation, and so on. All of those things provided for under the defence plan. What needed to be carried out and how. Of course the security situation also was assessed at the time in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did General Djordjevic participate in that meeting, or did he make any presentations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djordjevic was there. He did attend. I cannot remember now if General Djordjevic on that occasion said anything. But the practice at the MUP was that after the minister's address, nobody else would speak. So I remember very well that the head of the MUP staff in Pristina on that occasion welcomed all those present and thanked the minister for visiting. The minister then spoke. This is all recorded even in more detail then I shared just now. So I don't recall if anybody spoke after the minister, but the practice at the ministry was that after the minister, nobody else would address the gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there was a meeting of the 16th of April, 1999. Who, if you recall, were the attendees of that meeting and where was it held?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On April 16th, 1999, there was a meeting of the MUP staff in Pristina and I recall who attended this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who? Just say more senior people, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the most senior leaders, on behalf of the MUP, there was the Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic; head of the public security sector, Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic. From political structures there was president of the temporary Executive Council of Kosovo, Mr. Zoran Andjelkovic; and president of the provincial socialist party of Serbia branch, Mr. Zivkovic. Voja Zivkovic. Obviously I'm not pointing this out because this is clear enough since this was the MUP staff meeting, the leader of the MUP staff was obviously always present and this was General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were the SUP chiefs as well as the leaders of the detachments in Kosovo also present?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, SUP chiefs were also present, but I'm not including the SUP chiefs among the top leadership of the ministry because these are not elected officials, these are appointed personnel as anybody else is in the ministry. So I was talking about the top leadership, so those that were elected or appointed to high positions in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I -- can you just tell us in one sentence what were the topics that were discussed at this meeting? I just want to move quickly, that's why I ask you that way.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two topics: the current political and security situation in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and related tasks, and also personnel changes in certain Secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija. The second item of the agenda was discussed first and these were changes of chiefs of SUPs in Kosovo and Metohija. And this regarded SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica, SUP in Pristina, and SUP in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did General Djordjevic participate in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Djordjevic stated this at this meeting that chiefs of Secretariats who were sent from Serbia to act as chiefs of Secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija - talking here about the chiefs of SUPs in Kosovska Mitrovica and Pristina - have completed their respective tasks, and their duty was terminated as of 16th of April, but they were to stay in Kosovo and Metohija until the 30th of April to transfer their duties to the newly appointed chiefs of SUPs. And also the chief of SUP in Urosevac was replaced, Bogoljub Janicijevic was appointed as chief of SUP in Pristina, and a new person was appointed chief of SUP in Urosevac. In Kosovska Mitrovica, Vucina Janicevic was appointed chief of SUP who was previously chief of OUP in Vucitrn. This decision on appointment of new chiefs of SUP was handed down in person by General Djordjevic, and the decision on the termination of their duties was also handed to us in person by General Djordjevic. So I received the decision on termination of my duties as chief of SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica with 30th of April, 1999; and this decision stated that I completed the tasks for which I was sent there and therefore in accordance with the Law on the Interior such a decision was made. So my position was terminated with this and I did not have any new position. And this was the first time I learned about this at this meeting. I didn't know about any personnel changes prior to this meeting, so I wasn't aware that I was going to be terminated at that position previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just, I'm not sure you told us, could you just, please, remind us, the meeting on the 8th of March, 1999, where was this held?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of March, 1999, the meeting was held at the MUP staff in Pristina, but there were different rooms. Sometimes the meeting would take place in a small room, sometimes in a larger room. Most probably due to the number of attendees, this particular meeting took place in a large room.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we just look at documents quickly since you referred to the appointments and transfers of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the appointment or transfer of General -- of Major-General Momcilo Stojanovic. I referred to him earlier in respect to the RPOs, and it's dated 5th of October, 1998. And signed by General Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This decision was signed by the assistant minister chief of the department Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic, but this is not an appointment. This is the decision to send General Momcilo Stojanovic to carry out special security tasks in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Momcilo Stojanovic was assistant minister in the public security sector, and before that he was head of the Secretariat in Pozarevac and I knew him in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what his responsibilities were in Kosovo when he served there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, that is in 1998, the Ministry of the Interior developed a programme of housing of employees of the ministry in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Given that the housing situation was very difficult, the ministry planned to construct several housing compounds for the employees of the ministry. In the territory of SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica, a building was supposed to be constructed with 50 apartments in it. And the documentation was completed; we even had a contract signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it from what you are saying that he had responsibilities in respect to logistics and housing in Kosovo, is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So in respect to housing since this was the reason why he was coming to SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica and this was the topic that we discussed with subcontractors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We saw in the minutes of the meeting of the 17th of February that he had been engaged to do or to meet with the heads of the RPOs along with Colonel Pesic. Do you know what his responsibilities were in respect to the RPOs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I said yesterday it wasn't Colonel Pesic, it was Captain Pesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Pesic was in charge of RPOs at the level of MUP staff in Pristina, and General Momcilo Stojanovic was in charge of the issues that I just mentioned. But in order to give particular importance to the considerations of the RPOs, it wouldn't be advisable to have just a captain talking to a colonel, a lieutenant-colonel, or a major, and for this reason, General Momcilo Stojanovic was involved in this. So this is my assumption that his role in this particular area was to give particular importance to these talks. And this is why he joined Captain Pesic in visiting all the Secretariats and in discussing the situation concerning RPOs. He analysed the situation and proposed certain measures in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could this letter of -- I think the witness said it was a decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a decision to assign General Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could that be received in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1044, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move on to 1884. That's 01884.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You discuss the assignment also of -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the wrong document. That's the document we dealt with yesterday. I'm so sorry. The document I'm looking for is 01886. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is this the assignment or re-assignment of General -- sorry, of Mr. Petric signed by General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is a document that stipulates that Colonel Bosko Petric, that his duties of chief of the Secretariat in Pristina are terminated. So this is not a re-assignment or assignment, this is the termination of his duty. Previously, Bosko Petric was head of SUP in Uzice. From there he was transferred or re-assigned as chief of SUP in Pristina. And on 30th of April he was terminated at that duty, just as I was terminated at the duty of the chief of SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on, excuse me, Mr. Cvetic, to 04199.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For fear of mischaracterising, I'll just ask you what is it and who is it signed by?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a decision whereby Captain Milan Cankovic, employee of the Ministry of the Interior, to cease to carry out special security-related tasks in the MUP staff in Pristina, where he was deployed on 1st of May, 1998. So this is the same decision as the ones we saw for the previous two chiefs of Secretariats. It was made on the basis of the same legal document and signed by the same person, and this was assistant minister chief of the public security department, Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And 01890, if we could look at that quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this one is, could you tell us, Mr. Cvetic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the same decision as the previous one. It just refers to a different person and again signed by the same person and that is head of the public security department. So the decision for Colonel Miroslav Mijatovic whose duties cease, and these are the duties related to security tasks in Kosovo and Metohija, where he was deployed on 7th of July, 1998, signed by assistant minister head of public security department Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the same type of decision whereby Major Radovan Vucurevic's duty ceases, so the duties and tasks of assistant head of the Ministry of the Interior staff of Kosovo. I knew about this person, but I didn't know him firsthand. I didn't know him in person. The decision once again was signed by Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic, and this is indeed his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And lastly in this vein, 01888.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you go on, please?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision, but this time to send Lieutenant-Colonel Milenko Arsenijevic, an employee of the Ministry of Interior, to perform tasks and duties in the Pristina staff of the Ministry of Interior in the autonomous province of the Kosovo and Metohija, the decision is signed by assistant minister General Djordjevic. So the previous ones were decisions to terminate somebody's duty, and this one is a decision to send somebody to perform certain tasks and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If we could return now, Mr. Cvetic, to the MUP staff and their meetings in 1999. Do you recall a MUP staff meeting of the 17th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And who were the leading figures present at that one?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting there was General Lukic and heads of Secretariats and commanders of PJPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did General Lukic issue any orders or statements in respect to the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among other things, he also talked about volunteers. At that meeting, General Lukic said that the talks at Rambouillet were burdened with problems and that NATO forces were being accumulated in the territory of Macedonia. Therefore, that there was a threat of an aggression. Also that a signal of an imminent threat of aggression would be if the OSCE mission withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija. For that reason, it was necessary to prepare everything to mobilise reserve police forces so that the ratio between the active police forces and reserve police forces would be 1:1. In the territory of SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica, this meant the following: Given that we had 665 members of the police, we had to mobilise the same number of reserve policemen in order to satisfy the ratio of 1:1. He said that if the OSCE mission withdrew from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, this would be the first signal of the beginning of the NATO aggression. And in that respect, it was necessary to start bringing A and B formations of the Special Police to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. He also addressed other issues pertaining to the defence of civilian population in Kosovo and Metohija. And he also mentioned volunteers. When it comes to volunteers, Mr. Lukic stated the following: If there should be any volunteers in a certain territory, they should be kept in that territory, and once the NATO aggression starts, they should be included into the reserve forces of the Ministry of the Interior. So this was his position concerning the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said you left Kosovo in mid-April.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I left --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, sorry.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a MUP staff meeting in Pristina held on April the 16th, my duty was terminated, or actually, I can't really say that I was relieved of duty, but I was withdrawn from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija because the statement of reasons of that decision stipulate that I completed the duties and tasks for which I was sent there. But according to this decision, I stayed in Kosovo until the 30th of April. However, I transferred my duties to my successor around the 20th of April, and I physically left the area of Kosovo and Metohija on April the 28th. Obviously all this in line with the decisions of my superiors. And the same thing was done by the previous chief of SUP in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I wonder if this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we will have the first break now, and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, I wonder whether you could entertain us while we are waiting for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent, Your Honours. I don't want to influence him, so on page 4, line 27, there was a complete answer where the witness said that Mr. Lukic allowed him to leave Mitrovica in late April sometime.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is -- sorry, line 4, page 27 of the transcript. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, I'm going to stop now because the witness is coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, I'd like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this document is P771. 65 ter number 01996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the MUP staff meeting of the 7th of May, 1999. And if you look quickly at the participants, can you say whether or not these were the persons who normally attend the MUP staff meetings? I mean, where they are listed from one to ten.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 16th I was discharged from duty. On the 17th I left the territory of Kosovo, and this is minutes of the 7th of May when I was no longer in Kosovo and Metohija. As for the people listed here, I can say which ones attended the MUP staff meetings before, the ones that I also attended. I didn't attend this particular one. Earlier when I attending the meetings, until the 16th of April, 1999, were attended by -- this is the 1997, 1998, and April 1999 period, you would have Lieutenant-General Stojanovic; Mijatovic, Miroslav; Dragan. Then there was the general who was the head of the staff, then we would have Captain Pesic, Blagoje; Janicijevic, Bogoljub; Colonel Vlahovic, Borislav; Colonel Milos Vojnovic; Colonel Bilic [phoen], Bozidar; and Colonel Dusan Gavranic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could -- if we could look at page 11 in the English, and that is page 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the middle of the English copy, we have here on this I could indicate its part of the presentation of General Stevanovic, he says: "An organisation of work, the Secretariat of the Interior must ensure that in Kosovo and Metohija the organisation is such that all PJPs are subordinated to the chief of the Secretariat." And further on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is at the top of page 10 in B/C/S, if you could move there but remain on the same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He says: "On the 8th and 9th of May, 1999, set up and hold meetings for the entire leadership in the Kosovo and Metohija SUP. Hold regular SUP staff meetings in the coming period which must be attended by the entire leadership regardless of their responsibilities. The commanders of the A and B detachments are subordinated to the chief of SUP and must attend such meetings." Can you clarify this for us, what were the responsibilities of the chief of the SUP in respect to the A and B detachments of the PJPs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In advance, for process of prevention, if this refers to the period that the witness is familiar with in relation to these minutes, I don't think there's a problem for him to respond to any question. But if this was just a basis to have the question put to him, then it's all right. But I don't think that the witness should be the one to interpret the minutes because he himself said that he didn't attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is a chief of a SUP. He should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness will give his understanding in answer to your question. If Mr. Djurdjic thinks that is not adequate, he can deal with it in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvetic, do I need to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The second question -- to the second question because the first question I didn't have on the monitor. The first question where it says that on the 8th and 9th of May, 1999, meetings were organised in the SUP with the participation of the complete leadership and that these meetings should be attended by the commander of the A and B formations and that they should be subordinated to the SUP, I would like to say the following: Even before this date, the chief of the Secretariat of Internal Affairs did hold meetings with commanders of the PJP of the A and B formations. These meetings were devoted to the topic of how the units, especially the units, should be equipped, supported logistically, do they need medical support, what do these units need in terms of assistance. Do they need fuels, lubrication, weapons, vehicles. This is what the topics of the meetings were with the commanders of the PJP police units. So these questions were more of a logistical nature. There were also questions relating to the coverage of the territory when there were no anti-terrorist actions. What does that mean, "to cover the territory"? This means that then the PJP units, when they were not participating in the operations as manoeuvring structures, they participated as territorial units in supporting certain vital facilities such as bakeries, milk production plants, roads, some key media centres, and other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when they participated or as territorial units, to whom were they subordinated, and when they were engaged as manoeuvre units, to whom were they subordinated?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the PJPs participated in anti-terrorist actions as units in the territorial structure, they were subordinated to the MUP staff in Pristina. When the PJP units were acting as such, they didn't implement actions. They had to do something. They couldn't be in barracks all the time just to sit in these facilities. They were on patrol duty, security at check-points, security of facilities, and so on. This staff was then subordinated to the PJP commander. And the PJP commander exclusively issued assignments to those units. It was normal for the PJP commander and the chief of the Secretariat to meet and to discuss and agree on assignments that they were supposed to implement, but these were peacetime assignments of the Secretariat arising from the authority of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. These were not any actions but just regular tasks of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at document 01070. If we could just pause briefly on the front page and move to page 36 of the English. Sorry, 1074. Probably could move to the next page. Do we have a copy in B/C/S? Perhaps we could hand -- and for the -- and could we move to page 36 in English and 26 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: See here it says -- well, firstly, you have a copy of the document. Is that a document that the SUPs would normally have to prepare on a yearly basis? Are you familiar with documents of that nature? Maybe I should put the question that way.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said yesterday that based on the department's programme of work, every Secretariat in the Republic of Serbia adopts an annual work-plan, and this is an annual work-plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. We see here that there the SUP made plans in respect to the PJP units and here we see a plan is to: "Implement training plans for members of Special Police units active under force -- reserve forces for the 1st and 8th Company of the 124th Intervention Brigade of the PJP; the 1st Company of the 74th PJP Detachment of the active; and 1st and 2nd Companies of the 54th PJP Detachment of the reserve of the Pristina SUP according to the programme of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia." And were the SUPs responsible to implement training programs for PJP units that were attached to the SUPs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I must explain here how the PJP units were formed. I think that here we have a small misunderstanding. Namely, the PJP units at the level of the MUP were formed from personnel of all Secretariats in the Republic of Serbia of which there were 33 in total. All MUP Secretariats provided some personnel for those PJP units. Those PJP units were formed in detachments, and there were seven of them in total: two in Belgrade, one in Novi Sad, one in Uzice, one in Kragujevac, one in Nis, and one in Pristina. So all Secretariats in the SUP area of Kosovo and Metohija provided a certain number of personnel for the PJP Kosovo Detachment which later in June 1998 turned into the 124th Intervention Brigade. These -- this personnel when it's not on detachment activities have to be trained, they have to be equipped. And in that period of the year, the work-plan of the Secretariat pursuant to the ministry work-plan and the training plan for the PJP units, which the ministry of MUP sends to the Secretariats is implemented throughout the whole year. This training is implemented throughout the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this both applies to the active force and the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, I think we have to move on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 0174 -- could that be received, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1045, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P345, that is 0993. Sorry, 01993 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the minutes of another meeting of the police commanders in Kosovo on the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could go to page 8 in English, item 5. And it's at page 6 in B/C/S. And I think it is the last -- I'm sorry, we should just move to the end of the document, the last paragraph of the document because I see here in English it goes from page 8 to page 9. So could we look at the last paragraph on page 8 and then move on to page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is a presentation of Major-General Lukic, and he says: "Due to some problems with uniforms, a full check will be kept on the wearing of the police uniforms. Persons who are not members of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor slow down while reading, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "Persons who are not members of the police with P status and do not belong to reserve police units when mobilised are not allowed to wear police uniforms. Only PJP members may wear green uniforms in the course of the anti-terrorist action. Reserve police," what should be squad, "Reserve police squad members are not allowed to wear police or military uniforms if they are not mobilised and engaged in reserve police -- in reserve MUP or VJ units." What did he mean when he said -- when he referred to P status?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: P is police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were -- up until the time you left, were the reserve police - and when I say reserve police, I mean members of the active police who were reservists and not members of the reserve police units or squads - were there sufficient uniforms for all who had been mobilised in February and March?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't enough. I mean, there were uniforms with police insignia as well, but only members of the reserve forces of the police while they were mobilised. When they were engaged. Members of the active forces wore uniforms with police insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not sure if I understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness referred to the words in B/C/S "milicija" and "policija." Militia and police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Active police forces on the 5th of April, 1996, began to wear uniforms with insignia "policija," police. Why? Because on that date the name "milicija" was substituted with the name "policija." And because of that on the 5th of April, 1996, all members of the active forces had to have uniforms that had the insignia with the word "policija" on them. So these are new uniforms. The old uniforms which still had the "milicija" insignia were withdrawn, but the uniforms from that batch were still in the possession at home of members of the reserve forces. And for a while, they couldn't even change their uniforms. There was a plan of exchange of uniforms which first encompassed the active forces and then the reserve forces. This was due to financial reasons and also because the manufacturers were unable to produce all the required uniforms within a certain period of time. Because each policeman had three kinds of uniform: The first one was a formal uniform, then there was a work uniform, and the third was the intervention uniform. All these types of uniforms are subject to use which is laid down in the regulations on the use and manner of wearing of uniforms in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. And when you mobilised this very large number of reserve police officers in March, 1999, did all of them wear the uniforms with the "policija" insignia, or were there exceptions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they also wore uniforms with the insignia of "milicija."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to a different topic. I'd like us to look at some orders that were issued to the SUPs but various entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at 04164.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a dispatch from the head of the staff Major Lukic, and it's in respect to how the KVM should be treated after Mr. Walker, Mr. William Walker, the head was the persona non grata. That's the 24th of January, 1999. You remember these events and the circulation of this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I received it through our communications so it was encoded, it came from teleprinter centre, and it was handed over to heads of Secretariat in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. And heads of Secretariat were obliged to inform all the commanders of the police stations, all the heads of the interior of the OUPs in their territories about this; and the commanders of police stations and heads of OUPs were obliged to inform all of their police forces and all the persons that were coming in touch with members of the OSCE mission about this. So it was a very professional and correct treatment that was ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, I apologise, this was possibly the result of the fact that there were some members ever the police who did not act in this way, who did not behave in this way, and this is why it was requested that all the police forces should treat the OSCE mission in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see here that it's also addressed to the PJP Detachment commander. Anyway, let's look at the last paragraph: "All measures and instructions ordered to date in the dispatches of the MUP in the Republic of Serbia and the MUP staff in Pristina remain in force." Can you comment on that? This paragraph seems to indicate that the addressees, that is, the SUP chiefs and the command of the PJPs were getting orders both from the MUP staff in Pristina and the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, Belgrade. Can you comment on that? Is that what was occurring at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was happening for the dispatches to be sent directly from the Ministry of the Interior to the Secretariats in Kosovo and sometimes the dispatches were sent through MUP staff in Pristina. And also the MUP staff in Pristina could send out its own dispatches to the Secretariats in Pristina. And the Secretariats also reported back to the MUP staff in Pristina and to certain administrations at the level of the ministry of the Republic of Serbia. So the dispatches could come directly from the ministry, or they could be sent through the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could this document be received in evidence and given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1046, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could we look briefly at 4147.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does this appear to be another dispatch from the chief of the staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph Major-General Lukic says: "Any member of the police who does not obey the issued order shall be held accountable." In what ways could Major-General Lukic hold these persons accountable?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Major-General Lukic in this dispatch stated that any -- that any deviation from the orders as issued would imply responsibility, but that responsibility or to establish that responsibility you had to undertake certain procedure. And these were the following types of responsibility: First of all, disciplinary responsibility, misdemeanour responsibility, or criminal responsibility. So depending on the severity of an infringement, one would have a certain level of responsibility. So if we are talking about disciplinary responsibility, there could be violations of the duty which were smaller or more significant and they were determined in a regulation on the activities of the employees of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to get to the disciplinary provisions shortly, Mr. Cvetic. What I want to know is whether or not Major Lukic could discipline and hold the SUP chiefs and the other addressees responsible or accountable, as he put it, in his own right as Chief of Staff, or would he have to invoke the powers of the headquarters in Belgrade to hold anyone accountable?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we are talking about chiefs of SUPs, the leader of the MUP staff in Pristina could not instigate any disciplinary proceedings against them, but he could propose to the head of the sector, obviously given the reasoning and justification for this request, he could ask the security chief to instigate proceedings against SUP chiefs. When we are talking about other employees of the police, report on the infringement in the course of their duties was submitted by their immediate superiors to the chiefs of the Secretariats. And chief of the Secretariats would then request from the Prosecutor to initiate disciplinary proceedings. Following these disciplinary proceedings, the Prosecutor would submit a request to the court. In every single Secretariat we had the first-instance court and there was a higher-instance court at the level of the ministry. So disciplinary responsibility of members of the police was established through the Secretariat and not through the MUP staff. So legally it couldn't be done through the MUP staff because these particular personnel was not linked organisation-wise to the MUP staff, but they were deployed to the Secretariats and it was only Secretariats that could instigate disciplinary procedures. So General Lukic could suggest that disciplinary procedures be instigated against certain persons to the Secretariat chiefs, but he could not instigate these procedures himself. At least at the time when I was there, such were the laws and regulations regulating this particular topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move on to the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm reminded that this is a document that we should ask -- we should tender, Your Honour, that's 4167. Could it be received in evidence and given an exhibit number. May I just inquire, did we tender 4147?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which document is 4147?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could that be received in evidence, I think I used it earlier with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to tender both of them, Your Honours. I was probably trying to move a little bit too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Each will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 4164 will be -- apologies. 65 ter 4167 will become Exhibit P1047; and 4147 will become Exhibit P1048.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we seem to have a problem. Mr. Stamp misquoted a number under 65 ter list. This document 04167 was already admitted, and the 65 ter number 04147 still needs to be admitted into evidence, so I believe that we must have skipped a number between 1046 and 1048. I believe that we skipped one number and possibly the mistake was because the number under 65 ter list I believe was misquoted by Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit 1046, P1046, was Rule 65 ter 4164.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then two exhibits following that have been tendered as the Court Officer indicated. They are Rule 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps the concerns might be sorted out, and so if I just show the witness 4167, which I think is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Has not been shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps we should dispense with the witness and merely have you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's the problem of time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a quick look at 4167, Mr. Cvetic. And it is an example of another order from the MUP staff that I had wanted to show to you. If you look at page 2 in the English at item 7 we see that General Lukic is issuing clear orders to SUP chiefs and chiefs of the Crime Police Department. Is that the situation as it was while you were there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was not the time while I was chief of SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica. This was issued on 8th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that, but can you see from item 7 that General Lukic is issuing instructions and this is an example of him issuing instructions to SUP chiefs and members of the Crime Police Department?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under item 7 I can see that the other was to undertake all measures and activities pursuant to the provisions of laws and bylaws which are applicable in the state of war conditions. But there is nothing specific as to which laws and bylaws he was referring to. This is an exceptionally general formulation. So in my mind, this doesn't really mean anything. All measures and activities pertaining to what particular issue? What laws, what bylaws is he referring to? You have to be very specific. This is a very general formulation, and I couldn't really comment on it because there is nothing specific that this particular item refers to. Neither when we are talking about laws nor bylaws.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Cvetic. If we could move on to the issue of discipline which you mentioned, disciplinary proceedings within the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I should indicate that 1067 had already been given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it became Exhibit P1047, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the time you were in Kosovo up until the end of April, did the civilian criminal courts function?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did the tribunals for -- the MUP tribunals for internal disciplinary matters or breaches of discipline within the police force, were they functioning as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where there were allegations or information that a police officer had committed a crime, a serious crime like murder or robbery or rape or looting, how would this be treated by his superiors, or what would be the proper way to treat it if that information came to their attention?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about these criminal offences and if we were talking about the police officer, once his immediate superior - so the commander or the chief of the police department - when he learned about this would immediately inform the chief of the Secretariat. The chief of the Secretariat would immediately order that all the relevant evidence be collected. Now, it would all depend on whether this is just the first information or whether we already had firm evidence. If we had evidence pointing to this criminal offence, then the chief of the Secretariat would request from the chief of the relevant administration, in this case police administration, to approve that criminal a procedure be instigated. The chief of the Secretariat would submit criminal report to the competent Prosecutor for this alleged crime. At the same time, disciplinary procedure would be instigated for the disciplinary breach of duty and the particular perpetrator would be suspended until the completion of the procedures. He would be banned from coming to the Secretariat. His official documents and his official uniform would be taken away until the court procedure is completed. The chief of the Secretariat could not do any of this on its own without the approval of the chief of the police administration or the head of the sector. The same it true if the perpetrator was a traffic policemen or a crime policemen, so any other employees that belonged to the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And we are talking about criminal actions now. The governing law in respect to the crimes at that time was the Republic of Serbia criminal court; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, The Criminal Code, and the Criminal Procedure Act.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is P50 already in evidence, Your Honours, I would have looked at a couple of provisions, but I think we should proceed without that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say the chief of the Secretariat could not do any of this without the approval of the chief of the police administration or the head of the sector. Just to be sure, the chief of the police administration would be the chief of the police administration at the headquarters in Belgrade, and the head of the Secretariat would be the head of the public security sector; is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And in those circumstances, the headquarters in Belgrade ought to be and would be aware of all criminal proceedings against police officers in Kosovo if and when they were taking place?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only in Kosovo, but in the territory of the entire Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at document 01016. The decree on disciplinary responsibility of the Ministry of Interior. And if you could go to Articles 8 -- I beg your pardon. Okay. Fine. Let's just go straight to Article 10, which is at page 4 of the English, page 2 of the B/C/S. Oh, there it is. Article 10, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And basically, these are the -- this relates to how proceedings are initiated when there are serious breaches.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when any of those breaches, serious breaches, were alleged, could these proceedings be initiated or could the motion for disciplinary proceedings be submitted -- or withdrawn. Let me ask a more open question. Did the supervising officer who would submit the motion for disciplinary proceedings need the approval of the authorities in Belgrade to proceed with the motion for serious breaches?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only in two cases. If the violation was of such a type that it demanded for the person to be suspended, and in the second case when the alleged crime was a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you meant when the alleged breach of discipline was a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, disciplinary proceedings are conducted in case of criminal proceedings as well. The initiation of criminal proceedings does not actually stand instead of the disciplinary proceedings. It's not a substitute for it. Both proceedings have to be conducted, disciplinary proceedings, in order for the person to be removed from the organ until the criminal proceedings are completed and the criminal proceedings are conducted before the authorised court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could this document 01016, the decree on disciplinary responsibility, be received in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1049, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could we look at 04065. And if we could, in the B/C/S copy, go to the end. Not of that page, the end of the document, the last page of the document at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a dispatch of the public security department of the Ministry of Interior of the 9th of April, 1999. Signed by whom, is it, Mr. Cvetic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was signed by deputy minister, the chief of the department, Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you say deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could go back to the front page, the first page in English and have a look at the addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the question is this, because I think you've had an opportunity to peruse this dispatch recently: What were the responsibilities of the chief of the public sector department to ensure that the structure and operations of the police disciplinary system functioned smoothly and effectively.

utterances.speaker: LJUBINKO CVETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the public security department as the leader or at the head -- person at the head of the department, whereas the leadership function of the department implies also a control function. He had to implement also work on the functioning of the disciplinary proceedings and courts. What was presented here, though, indicates that the chief of the department only informed by dispatch his internal organisational units, units which are part of the department that in the "Official Gazette" number 17 dated the 7th of April, 1999, the decree on Internal Affairs was published in times of war.
